title: FIA confirm Williams’ minor overspend breach of 2025 Cost Cap
excerpt:
Formula 1's governing body the FIA have completed their review of the F1 teams’ and power unit manufacturers’ compliance with the 2025 Financial Regulations, with Williams found to have committed an unintentional minor overspend breach and a procedural breach, while Alpine also made a procedural breach.

As part of the review by the Cost Cap Administration (CCA) – a process that took eight months – all 11 Formula 1 teams and all five power unit (PU) manufacturers submitted financial documentation from 2025.

Nine of the 11 teams and all five power unit manufacturers were found in compliance for 2025, but Williams were found to have unintentionally committed a minor overspend breach and a procedural breach.

In a document confirming that an Accepted Breach Agreement (ABA) has been entered into between Williams and the Cost Cap Administration, it was explained that “there is no evidence that WGPE [Williams Grand Prix Engineering] gained or sought to gain any advantage (sporting or otherwise) from the identified breaches”, and that “the minor overspend breach amounts to £627k and therefore, with 0.48% over the 2025 Cost Cap, falls at the lower end of the <5% minor overspend range”.

Williams will subsequently pay a financial penalty for the breach, as well as taking a 1.5% reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.

The team said in a statement: “The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

“The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

“Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future. We have always been and will continue to be strong supporters of the Cost Cap, which naturally requires accurate policing to be effective.”

A procedural breach was identified for Alpine, with the FIA confirming that “there is no evidence that Alpine gained or sought to gain any advantage from the inaccurate exclusions or adjustments of certain costs; and notwithstanding the Cost Cap Administration’s determination of procedural breach, Alpine’s relevant costs in respect of the 2025 Reporting Period were below the 2025 Cost Cap”.

An Accepted Breach Agreement has been entered into between the team and the Cost Cap Administration, with Alpine set to pay a financial penalty and bear the costs incurred by the Cost Cap Administration in connection with its investigation of the Procedural Breach and the preparation of the ABA.

title: 5 storylines we're excited about ahead of the Qatar GP
excerpt:
Fresh from one of the most exciting races in recent memory, it’s time to shift focus to the Gulf for the final two rounds of the 2026 season. There wasn’t only great racing to talk about after Las Vegas, but frustrations and controversies among teams and drivers that could still be simmering under the surface as we make the trip to Qatar.

Verstappen and Russell’s rift

Tensions rose in Las Vegas during the final practice session of the weekend, particularly between Max Verstappen and George Russell.

With the first two sessions impacted by rain, and no dry running possible, FP3 was a busy session with drivers looking to get as much data as they could before locking in their set-ups ahead of qualifying. That led to a moment where Russell and Verstappen fought on track, and Russell later spoke out against the Dutchman's approach.

“I’m not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they’re bigger and better than everyone else,” Russell said. “Somebody has got to stand up to that guy.”

The pair started alongside each other on the front row and delivered a thrilling fight in a remarkable race until Russell hit the barrier trying to overtake team mate Kimi Antonelli, with Verstappen going on to secure his fourth victory in six races.

Following his win, Verstappen was then asked about Russell’s comments and was similarly in no mood to smooth over relations.

“He speaks a lot next to the track,” Verstappen said. “And honestly, for me, it doesn’t really bother me, because he’s so far below my level, it doesn’t make sense for me anyway to try and challenge that. So it doesn’t bother me.

“And, today, karma is a b****. It was honestly fantastic when I looked in my mirror and I saw what was happening [when Russell hit the wall]. I was like, ‘fantastic, my day is only getting better’. And then when I crossed the line in first, my day was complete.”

Qatar was the scene of a disagreement between the two drivers back in 2024, after Verstappen was given a grid penalty for impeding Russell during Qualifying. Verstappen said he “lost all respect” for Russell following the stewards’ hearing, and they now return to the scene of that incident after another verbal joust.

Driver drama at Ferrari

If Russell was frustrated with the way his race panned out in Las Vegas, then so too was his former team mate Lewis Hamilton after an incident-filled Saturday night.

Hamilton was penalised for leaving the track at Turn 7 and gaining an advantage in a fight with Lando Norris in the first half of the race, before then being hit by team mate Charles Leclerc at the same corner later on.

PALMER: Where do Ferrari go from here after Las Vegas clash?

The contact tapped Hamilton into a spin and limited him to seventh place at the flag, with Leclerc earning his own 10-second time penalty for the collision and being demoted to tenth place.

Team Principal Fred Vasseur described the incident as “more than unacceptable” and accused Leclerc of a lack of respect, with the fact he had spoken to both drivers after their battle in Mexico City only adding to Vasseur’s frustration.

The inference was he would take his time before working out his next move, and Thursday will be the first chance to hear from the drivers if there have been any repercussions.

Bearman’s contractual situation at Haas

Following the confirmation in the run-up to the Las Vegas Grand Prix that Liam Lawson, Arvid Lindblad and Valtteri Bottas are all retaining their seats for 2027, only one position remains unconfirmed.

That’s the place of Ollie Bearman at Haas, where at the time of writing a formal announcement has yet to be forthcoming.

Bearman will still race for Haas next season, and confirmation is expected imminently, but the 21-year-old was clearly frustrated when he spoke to the media in Las Vegas, expressing his disappointment and saying there is “no excuse” for his contract to still have been unsigned.

Once there is an official announcement, it will be interesting to see if Bearman can offer any further insight into what was causing the delay, with his future slightly more complex than some drivers as it involves both Ferrari and Haas at this stage.

Komatsu insists there is 'no doubt' over Bearman's Haas seat

Camara forgoes F2 title bid

While Bearman was still waiting to be able to confirm his future, his team mate received certainty over his own plans.

Rafael Camara made his Haas debut at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix and retained his seat in Las Vegas, as the team decided how to move forward following the sidelining of Esteban Ocon. While Camara was only announced for Las Vegas in the build-up to that race, the lack of news regarding the remaining two rounds suggested there was an outside chance he could still return to Formula 2 to try and defend his championship lead.

That notion has now been put to bed, with Camara confirmed in the Haas for the remainder of this season, ahead of his full-time drive in 2027.

F2 regulations state a driver cannot also compete in F1 in the same weekend, so Camara will now be unable to add to his points tally in the feeder series, and is likely to see one of Nikola Tsolov or Alex Dunne take the championship ahead of him.

A high speed test and minimum two-stop

The Lusail International Circuit could not be much different from the Las Vegas Strip Circuit when it comes to track characteristics. Aside from being a night race, the two share few similarities.

A much warmer climate awaits this weekend, but the drivers will also be having to work hard through the numerous high speed corners that push a car to the limits of its aerodynamic performance. The track surface is also extremely rough compared to Las Vegas, and there are some punishing kerbs if you run over them on too many occasions.

Last year, Pirelli imposed a maximum lap count of 25 laps per tyre set in Qatar, due to the energy loads, thermal stress and tread wear that the track creates. This time around, that limit has been increased to 27 laps per set, but with a 57-lap race it means it will still be impossible to complete the distance without changing tyres on two occasions.

Laps in every session count and the total is cumulative, but the reconnaissance laps to the grid and formation lap will not be included in the total, nor will any laps after the chequered flag.

title: Jack Whitehall on why Antonelli surprised him in first meeting
excerpt:
Jack Whitehall has shared the story of how Kimi Antonelli took him by surprise when they first met, with the actor and comedian insisting that the new World Champion is “not like any sportsman I’ve ever interacted with”.

After hosting F1-75 Live at the start of the 2025 season, Whitehall has since become an official Friend of F1 and even participated in the recent LEGO race held at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Briton has also collaborated with Mercedes as part of a series for the team’s partner Marriott Bonvoy, meaning that he has been able to spend time with Antonelli and George Russell – and says he found himself surprised by Antonelli’s nature outside of the car.

“Because I’ve done over the last year a lot of work with Mercedes and I’ve been around them a lot, I have grown very fond of George and Kimi, and so it’s been really nice to be around them as they’ve had this kind of upturn in form,” Whitehall explained on the latest episode of official podcast F1 Beyond The Grid.

“Particularly with Kimi, watching him have this incredible season and being a little bit adjacent to it at times has been so amazing. He’s not like any sportsman that I’ve ever interacted with.

“I’ve done lots of stuff with footballers and rugby players, and there’s always an element of, I don’t know, ego and charisma. Not that Kimi doesn’t have charisma, but he’s just so unassuming and humble, and sweet and impish, and it’s insane.

“Something must just switch the minute he gets behind the wheel in that car and he just turns into an absolute beast.”

When asked if Antonelli is always pulling pranks – given that the Italian has become known for his fondness of a practical joke – Whitehall recounted the amusing story of when he first met the 20-year-old.

“He’s so silly and mischievous,” said Whitehall. “The first time I ever met with him, we were doing a little sketch in Singapore and we were filming in a hotel room.

“Everyone was kind of worried, and again this always happens when you’re filming with a sportsman – they’re all worried about whether they’re going to be in a good mood when they come in, and how long they’re going to have with you to do the little bit because they’ve got this insane schedule that they have to keep to.

“He came in, he walks in, he’s friendly to everyone, and genuinely all he was asking about was whether he could jump on the bed, because he wanted to jump up and down on the bed!

“And I was like ‘Is he doing a bit here? You’re literally like the Kimi Antonelli persona that I have in my head, and it’s just real’. He was just so unassuming, and he was grinning and fun.”

Whitehall also went on to share his experiences with other well-known names in F1 during the conversation, including Russell, Lewis Hamilton and Toto Wolff.

title: From Monza mayhem to Suzuka showdowns – 10 dramatic F1 rivalry flashpoints
excerpt:
Max Verstappen's sensational victory in the Las Vegas Grand Prix last weekend, where the Red Bull driver came out on top after a slipstream thriller, was given an extra edge after some on- and on-track tension with George Russell.

The pair battled for the win on the streets of Las Vegas having already gone wheel-to-wheel earlier in the weekend during practice, prompting comments from Russell in the press, with Verstappen firing back after his win.

It is the latest in a series of incidents between the two, but it taps into a long history of driver rivalries within Formula 1 which were triggered by some dramatic flashpoints...

Verstappen vs Russell: Contact in Catalunya

The war of words between Verstappen and Russell escalated to new heights over the Las Vegas weekend, with Verstappen having the final say after his win, claiming Russell to be "so far below my level".

It's certainly not the first time the pair have had issues with each other. During the Sprint at the 2023 Azerbaijan Grand Prix, the pair made contact on the opening lap at Turn 2, with Verstappen's Red Bull suffering floor damage and leading the Dutchman to confront Russell afterwards.

Just over a year later, their rivalry went up a notch as Verstappen was handed a grid penalty for the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix, losing his pole position after being deemed to have driven unnecessarily slowly on a cooldown lap.

Russell had been impeded in the process and ironically inherited pole, only for Verstappen to win the race and state that he had “lost all respect” for the Mercedes driver due to his comments in front of the stewards.

Things came to a head further at the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix, where after losing positions on a late Safety Car restart, Verstappen cut a corner to move back ahead of Russell.

Having been prompted to hand the position back by his team, Verstappen then launched his car up the inside of Russell and made heavy contact in a move which earned the four time champ a 10-second penalty.

Verstappen vs Hamilton: Copse clash

The battle for the 2021 title became one of the most infamous and controversial in the history of the championship, with protagonists Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton colliding on numerous occasions.

The pair went wheel-to-wheel in several early encounters, notably in Bahrain and the opening corners of the Emilia Romagna and Spanish GPs.

Their first major flashpoint came on the opening lap of the British GP, the pair making high-speed contact at Copse corner which sent Verstappen into the barrier hard, while Hamilton won after serving a penalty for the incident.

The pair came to blows again at the Italian GP through the opening chicane, with Verstappen landing on top of his rival after Hamilton had just exited the pits as both retired.

Hamilton got the better of Verstappen in the Sao Paulo GP after climbing up from the back of the grid, but only after the pair nearly collided again as they both went off track at Turn 4.

Several off-track moments and a further collision in the inaugural Saudi Arabian GP, won by Hamilton's Mercedes, all culminated in the pair entering the Abu Dhabi title decider tied on points.

The rivals battled hard on the opening lap once more with Hamilton coming out on top, before a late Safety Car ultimately handed Verstappen the chance to win his maiden F1 title after a fractious season.

Hamilton vs Rosberg: Lap 1 in Barcelona

With Mercedes entering the new-for-2014 regulations as the dominant force, the relationship between Hamilton and team mate Nico Rosberg was always likely to be strained as they battled for the title over a three-year period.

Hamilton proved victorious in the first season, the pair having collided in the 2014 Belgian GP, while tensions had already risen after the Briton accused Rosberg of deliberately bringing out a yellow flag in Qualifying for the Monaco GP, denying him a shot of pole.

Hamilton claimed the title again the following season at the US GP, having squeezed Rosberg on the exit of Turn 1 at the start. Tensions once again boiled over in the cooldown room, as Hamilton tossed the Pirelli podium cap at Rosberg, only for the German to angrily throw it back.

Rosberg beat Hamilton in 2016 – but only after the pair collided twice: famously on the opening lap of the Spanish GP as both were eliminated, while Rosberg lost a win in Austria as the Mercedes duo came to blows on the final lap.

The season culminated in Hamilton leading Rosberg at the Abu Dhabi finale, with Hamilton ignoring team orders and backing his team mate up into Sebastian Vettel and Verstappen behind.

It ultimately failed to make the difference as Rosberg claimed the tite before announcing his shock retirement just days later.

Vettel vs Webber: Tension in Turkey

Mark Webber and Sebastian Vettel's first coming together ocurred before they were even team mates, with the Australian already at Red Bull while the German was driving for Toro Rosso in his maiden season.

The pair were circulating in the podium positions in the monsoon at the 2007 Japanese Grand Prix, only for Vettel to drive into the back of Webber under a Safety Car as both retired.

The duo joined forces at Red Bull in 2009, before they each challenged for the title the following season where sparks began to fly. They crashed together again in the Turkish GP, with Vettel eliminated as the squad publicly sided with him.

The team divide soon began to become even more apparent, as a new front wing upgrade at the British GP was moved from Webber's car to Vettel's after the latter's had failed in practice.

Furious in the post-Qualifying press conference, Webber won the race before claiming over the radio, "not bad for a number two driver".

While Vettel would claim that year's crown on his way to four successive titles, there was one further flashpoint when the World Champion ignored the famous "multi-21" team orders and attacked Webber for the win at the 2013 Malaysian GP, prompting a cooldown room confrontation.

Hamilton vs Alonso: High drama in Hungary

Arriving at McLaren in 2007 as a double World Champion and placed alongside an F1 rookie, Fernando Alonso expected that a third title would soon be his.

Instead, the Spaniard endured a season of fighting his new team mate Hamilton, which ultimately meant both missed out on the title by a single point, as the team was also gripped by a Spygate scandal.

Tensions had begun to surface as early as Monaco, where Hamilton felt he was denied a chance of his maiden victory by team orders, although his first win in F1 soon came at the Canadian GP.

At the following round in the US, Alonso found that his biggest rival during the season was coming from inside the same team, as Hamilton refused to let the two-time World Champion ahead when battling for the lead.

Things came to a head in Qualifying for the Hungarian GP, with Alonso intentionally blocking his team mate in the pit box to prevent Hamilton from having enough time to set another fast lap.

Alonso was eventually handed a five-place grid penalty for his pit lane misdemeanor by the stewards.

The Spanish driver ultimately left the team at the end of the season after one of the most fractious relationships in F1 history.

Schumacher vs Villeneuve: The Jerez title decider

Despite just one point separating Michael Schumacher and Jaques Villeneuve heading to the final round of the 1997 season at the European GP, remarkably the pair had never shared the podium together that season.

That looked like finally changing in Jerez, as the two contenders – along with Heinz-Harald Frentzen – all set exactly the same lap time in Qualifying.

Schumacher jumped ahead of polesitter Villeneuve at the start and led through the pit stop phase but soon began to fall into the clutches of the Williams driver heading into the final third of the race.

Heading into a right-hand hairpin, Villeneuve saw his chance and launched himself up the inside, with Schumacher continuing to turn his Ferrari towards the apex.

The right-front wheel of Schumacher's car bounced off Villeneuve's sidepod, with the then two-time World Champion sent into the gravel on the exit of the corner and becoming beached.

Villeneuve was able to continue and reach the finish in third, which was enough to clinch the title – but the ramifications of Schumacher's actions were huge.

The FIA disqualified him from the season's standings after deeming his driving as a deliberate attempt to eliminate Villeneuve, and there was no love lost between the pair over the following seasons after the incident.

Schumacher vs Hill: Title climax controversy

Schumacher had already been at the centre of controversy on his way to winning his maiden drivers' title in the 1994 season with Benetton.

Like Jerez three years later, Schumacher entered the final round of the season in Australia with a one-point lead over another Williams driver – on this occasion Damon Hill.

Having taken the lead at the start on the streets of Adelaide, Schumacher continued to be pressured by Hill, with the German eventually making a mistake, running off the track and hitting the wall.

With broken suspension Schumacher rejoined the track as Hill looked to pass, the pair making contact at the next corner as Schumacher's Benetton was launched into the air and then the barrier. Hill continued back to the pits, but damaged suspension meant his title bid came to an end.

Schumacher claimed his second title more convincingly the following year in 1995, but the pair still collided twice at Silverstone and Monza, before Hill finally triumphed in 1996 after Schumacher moved to Ferrari.

Despite not challenging for the title again, Hill continued to have altercations with Schumacher until his retirement at the end of 1999, notably when being lapped at Suzuka in 1997 and while battling for position during the 1998 Canadian GP.

Senna vs Prost: Suzuka showdowns

Perhaps the most infamous rivalry in F1 history, Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost's acrimony towards each other began as early as their first season together in 1988 at McLaren.

At the Portuguese GP, Prost felt he was nearly pushed into the pit wall by Senna, who eventually claimed his first title as the relationship only deteriorated the following season.

The pair squabbled over an agreement made before the start of the 1989 San Marino GP, which prohibited overtaking before the Tosa corner on the opening lap. Prost had beaten his team mate off the line at a subsequent restart, only for Senna to pass before Tosa, claiming the deal was only for the first start.

The intra-team battle concluded with the pair colliding into the final chicane at the Japanese GP, allowing Prost to claim the title with Senna disqualified after winning the race on-the-road but having cut the chicane when rejoining.

Despite Prost moving to Ferrari for 1990, the rivalry still remained just as bitter and the championship was decided in Senna's favour, but only after a high-speed crash at the start in Suzuka wiped them both out of the race.

Relations remained fractious over the following seasons, as Prost even blocked Senna from joining him at Williams in 1993 as he claimed a fourth and final title.

The pair shared a final podium in Australia, as Prost's retirement opened the door for Senna to join Williams with the duo having reconciled their relationship before the Brazilian's death at Imola in 1994.

Mansell vs Piquet: War at Williams

When Nelson Piquet joined Williams for the 1986 season, the Brazilian had already won two titles with Brabham and expected preferential treatment at the team in his quest for a third accolade.

But Nigel Mansell had already settled in at the squad the previous season, and had became a multiple race winner – and a serious threat to Piquet's title ambitions.

While the pair battled on track and in the press, both tried to establish supremacy inside the team – a situation which was made more complex by owner Frank Williams being absent and confined to hospital after his car accident.

Despite a distinct lack of on-track collisions, the duo still took vital points off each other, which ultimately allowed Alain Prost to snatch the 1986 title with McLaren after Mansell suffered a spectacular tyre blowout at the final round in Australia.

Despite Mansell taking six wins against Piquet's three in 1987, including a surging charge at Silverstone to beat his team mate after an unscheduled pit stop, the title ultimately went to the Brazilian after Mansell suffered back injuries in a Japan practice crash.

Piquet would leave for Lotus at the end of the season, eventually moving to Benetton before retiring in 1991, while Mansell had a spell at Ferrari before returning to Williams and winning the title in 1992.

Villeneuve vs Pironi: A tragic end to a bitter rivalry

The 1982 season was filled with tragedy and 'what if' scenarios for Ferrari, as the Scuderia ended the season without Gilles Villeneuve, after the French-Canadian's death, while Didier Pironi's F1 career came to an abrupt end after an accident when on the cusp of the title.

The Ferrari 126C looked competitive compared with previous cars produced at Maranello, and with most of the grid boycotting the San Marino GP due to political reasons, Villeneuve and Pironi looked on course for a popular 1-2.

Villeneuve led once the main Renault opposition of Prost and Rene Arnoux had retired, and Ferrari informed their drivers to conserve fuel and slow down.

While Villeneuve took this to mean remain in order, Pironi began to battle his team mate, the Frenchman ultimately stealing the lead on the last lap for his first win with the team.

Villeneuve, who believed Pironi had only been battling earlier to entertain the tifosi and that victory was guaranteed, was furious and vowed never to speak with his team mate again.

Tragically he kept his word as, less than two weeks later, Villeneuve lost his life in a Qualifying accident ahead of the Belgian GP, while Pironi moved himself into the lead of the championship over the following races.

But a Qualifying accident of his own in the wet at Hockenheim severely injured both of Pironi's legs – and ended his F1 career. He ultimately lost out on the title by just five points after missing the final five races of the season.

Having taken up power boat racing after an F1 comeback proved impossible, Pironi would also eventually lose his life during a race in 1987.

title: What tyres will the teams have for the Qatar Grand Prix?
excerpt:
Formula 1 heads to the Lusail International Circuit for the penultimate round of the 2026 season this weekend, and tyre suppliers Pirelli have confirmed the compounds that the teams and drivers will have available to them for Round 22 on the calendar.

For the night race in Qatar, the C1, C2 and C3 have been selected as the hard, medium and soft compounds respectively, marking the hardest selection in Pirelli's range for a circuit characterised by high-speed corners and significant demands on the tyres.

Drivers will get two sets of the hard tyre (marked white), three sets of the medium tyre (marked yellow), and eight sets of the soft tyre (marked red), as well as access to the green intermediate tyre and the blue full wets, should they be required.

An extra set of softs is reserved for those who reach Q3 in Qualifying, while all drivers must use at least two different slick compounds during the race, providing the track is dry.

As was the case in 2025, a maximum number of laps will also be imposed on each set of tyres throughout the weekend, with the limit increased from 25 to 27 laps for this year's event.

The restriction has been introduced as a precautionary measure due to the high levels of energy, thermal stress and tyre wear generated by Lusail's demanding high-speed layout, helping to prevent tyres from being used beyond their safe operating limits.

The limit means drivers will be required to make at least two pit stops during the 57-lap Grand Prix, with the lap count calculated cumulatively across all sessions, including laps completed behind the Safety Car or Virtual Safety Car.

The increase from last year's 25-lap restriction reflects the lower loads recorded with the 2026 cars, along with further reinforcement of the tyre construction.

“The circuit features 16 corners and its high level of severity stems from the succession of high-speed turns, which subject the tyres to continuous stress for much of the lap,” reads Pirelli’s weekend preview. “The relatively smooth track surface and the high track temperatures can encourage graining on all compounds, a phenomenon that further increases wear.

“Despite operating in very demanding conditions, the tyres deliver consistent performance throughout the stint. Experience from previous years has shown that performance degradation remains relatively limited even when wear levels are high.

“To prevent tyres from being used beyond their intended life, managing degradation while placing excessive fatigue on the structure, Pirelli has introduced, in agreement with the FIA, a maximum stint length of 27 laps for each set. As a result, the race will inevitably be a minimum two-stop event for all drivers.

“The maximum lap limit has been increased compared to last year because the 2026 tyres feature a further reinforced construction and the cars generate lower levels of aerodynamic load than their 2025 predecessors.

“The introduction of this restriction, as an alternative to other measures such as increasing minimum starting pressures, will allow drivers to push harder during their stints, reducing the need for pace management.

"The absence of the Sprint format, which was in place last year, will also make life easier for the teams, both in managing the remaining mileage available on each tyre set and in fine-tuning their cars during free practice."

For more information about Pirelli’s F1 tyres, visit pirelli.com.

title: Why the Qatar GP is home to a unique and unusual F1 rule
excerpt:
The Qatar Grand Prix will see maximum tyre stints enforced throughout the weekend - but why is the rule in place?

Pirelli will once again enforce a maximum stint limit for the F1 tyres this weekend at the Qatar Grand Prix, which hosts the penultimate round of the season.

It is a move that it has adopted on several occasions in the past during the sport's visit to the Lusail International Circuit.

Maximum tyre stint limits exist as a safety measure, introduced by the FIA and Pirelli to prevent microscopic separation within the tyre carcass from developing into sudden deflation during high-speed running.

At Lusail specifically, the concern has centred on extreme localised front-tyre wear caused by sustained lateral loads and high carcass temperatures through the circuit's continuous fast corners, with Pirelli's evaluations showing that running beyond a set number of laps fully depletes the tread compound's protective layer and exposes the underlying structure to failure risk.

This year, it has increased the maximum permitted tyre stint length for the Qatar Grand Prix to 27 laps, up from 25 last year, with the change rooted in both the tyre construction and this year's cars.

The Italian manufacturer explained that the 2026 tyre range features a further reinforced internal carcass, built to resist fatigue despite being lighter than before.

Pirelli also condensed its dry compound range this year, dropping the softest C6 option to leave five choices from C1 to C5, with the harder end of that range dominating selection at Lusail.

[Article continues below]

Grand Prix

Qatar GP

Pirelli also pointed to the lower aerodynamic load generated by the 2026 generation of cars compared with their 2025 predecessors, reducing the peak cornering stresses that drive carcass wear and localised tread degradation through Lusail's sweeping, high-speed corners.

That drop in load is partly a product of the sport's new technical regulations, which have cut overall downforce by roughly 30 per cent through flatter floors that do away with the full Venturi ground-effect tunnels used between 2022 and 2025.

The cars have also become lighter and more compact, all of which chip away at the mechanical and aerodynamic forces that load up the tyres through Lusail's long, sweeping corners.

The restriction traces back to the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix. That led to an 18-lap stint cap being imposed that weekend.

Concerns over Lusail's demands on tyres stretch back further still, to the inaugural 2021 race, when four drivers suffered sudden front-left punctures amid the sustained lateral loads of the track's high-speed right-handers.

For Sunday's 57-lap race, the 27-lap ceiling still forces at least two pit stops, since two full stints cover only 54 laps. But the extra two laps per stint compared with 2025 widens the strategic window for teams, giving them more freedom to react to a Safety Car or stagger their stops rather than being locked into a rigid split.

With no scope to stretch a set beyond the limit, compound choice is expected to centre on outright pace and degradation resistance across three stints using the harder end of Pirelli's range, rather than any attempt at thermal conservation.

title: Liam Lawson sets 'very strong' Racing Bulls goal after securing F1 future
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has outlined what he wants to achieve with Racing Bulls next season, following confirmation that he will race for the team in F1 next season.

Liam Lawson has set his sights on keeping Racing Bulls at the head of the F1 midfield in 2027 after securing his seat for next season.

He believes the team’s ability to deliver upgrades that work as well on track as they do in the simulator has been central to its push for fifth in the constructors’ championship.

The New Zealander has also been one of the standout performers of 2026. He sits ninth in the drivers’ standings on 89 points, as best of the rest behind the top four teams, 37 clear of his nearest rival, Alpine's Pierre Gasly.

Yet whether Lawson would keep his place on the grid had become one of the main talking points in the driver market, with Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov in contention for his seat.

Racing Bulls ended the speculation on 12 November by retaining Lawson alongside Arvid Lindblad for 2027. Tsolov will serve as reserve driver for both Red Bull teams.

Asked what goals he had set himself for next year, Lawson told media, including RacingNews365: "I think maybe more of the same, really. We want to try and stay on top of the midfield if we can.

"Obviously, we still have some races to go this year, and we want to try and secure that, but to try and keep that momentum into next year and keep the development going."

[Article continues below]

Driver

Liam Lawson

New Zealander

30

Lawson outlines Racing Bulls 'target'

Neither Lawson nor Lindblad scored in the most recent grand prix, in Las Vegas, where Gasly finished fifth and Franco Colapinto sixth to collect 18 points for Alpine, cutting Racing Bulls' advantage from 45 points to 27.

It was the first time since Zandvoort, the first round back after the F1 summer break, that the Faenza-based squad failed to register a point.

With Qatar and Abu Dhabi to come, Racing Bulls leads Alpine by 114 points to 87. Holding on to fifth would give the team its best constructors' championship finish in a history stretching back to its days as Minardi.

"I feel like as a team, everything we've brought to the track this year, the upgrades have worked very, very well," Lawson added.

"It's not that easy sometimes to do that. You sometimes have upgraded simulations that show something that's going to work on a car, and it doesn't always do what you think it's going to do, but for us it has this year.

"I think that's where we've been very strong, and to try and keep that into next year, that's the target."

title: Alpine reveal cause of F1 cost cap breach as FIA sanction issued
excerpt:
Alpine has explained its procedural breach of the FIA cost cap rules for the 2025 F1 season, for which it has received a financial penalty from the motorsport governing body.

The team acknowledged and accepted the findings of the Cost Cap Administration (CAA) in a statement shared with media, including RacingNews365, shortly after the FIA announced its findings.

The Enstone-based squad entered into an Accepted Breach Agreement (ABA) with the FIA on 11 November 2026, which resulted in a fine. However, the amount has not been disclosed.

Alpine was found to have committed "errors and inaccuracies" in its reporting for the 2025 campaign, but as it did not breach the actual cost cap spending limit, it has not been subjected to a sporting punishment, unlike Williams.

The statement from the team spokesperson said: "Alpine Formula One Team acknowledges and accepts the findings of the Cost Cap Administration (CCA) for the 2025 Reporting Period.

"The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a Procedural Breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the Full Year Reporting Documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn’t give the team any performance advantage, such as Marketing Activities, non-F1 Activities, HR Activities, Employee’s Bonus Costs, Offsetting of Costs, and Costs of Inventories.

"The team would also like to express its thanks to both the CCA and FIA, for its diligence and understanding throughout the entire process.

"The Financial Regulations are still relatively new, constantly evolving and complex, with some exclusions and adjustments being open to each team’s interpretation. The team acknowledges the collective efforts it needs to make across the business and recognises where improvements can be made in future."

The CAA, meanwhile, stated: "The Cost Cap Administration recognised that Alpine has acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process and has sought to provide additional information and evidence when requested in a timely manner and that there is no accusation or evidence that Alpine has sought or obtained any undue advantage as a result of the Procedural Breach."

title: Williams learn FIA punishment after breaking F1 spending limits
excerpt:
Williams has issued a statement after being found to have broken F1's cost cap for the 2025 season.

The FIA, in its audit of the spending of every team and power unit manufacturer, found that nine of the 11 teams and all five PUMs were within the rules for the 2025 season.

Williams was found to have overspent and committed procedural breaches, whilst Alpine was found to have committed procedural breaches, but did not overspend.

Williams quickly issued a statement following the announcement confirming that it had overspent by £627,000 GBP - around 0.48% over the 2025 cost cap, which was $135 million USD, plus inflation. This is around £103 million GBP.

After breaching the rules, Williams has entered into an Accepted Breach Agreement with the FIA, where it will be fined and suffer a 1.5% reduction in its wind tunnel and CFD allocations over the next 12 months.

The overspend came as a result of "administrative costs" incurred during changes to the company structure, with the team wrongly believing these to fall outside the cost cap.

Following the news, the team issued the following statement.

"Williams F1 Team has reached an Accepted Breach Agreement with the FIA in relation to our 2025 Cost Cap submission.

"The FIA has determined that the team committed a minor overspend breach and an accompanying procedural breach, unintentionally exceeding the cap by £627,000 – 0.48% over the 2025 Cost Cap. The agreed outcome is a financial penalty and a 1.5% reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.

"The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure. We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted cooperatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future.

"We have always been and will continue to be strong supporters of the Cost Cap, which naturally requires accurate policing to be effective."

title: Two F1 teams found in breach of FIA cost cap regulations
excerpt:
Williams and Alpine have both fallen foul of the FIA cost cap rules for the 2025 F1 season, with the pair found to have committed procedural breaches. The Grove-based squad was also found to have slightly surpassed the spending limit.

Williams and Alpine have committed cost cap breaches for the 2025 F1 season, the FIA has confirmed ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix.

A minor overspend breach and a procedural breach were identified for the former, whilst the latter was found to have made a procedural breach.

Alpine has avoided significant punishment, but has been fined. Team Enstone acknowledged and accepted the findings of the Cost Cap Administration (CCA).

Meanwhile, Williams has been issued more considerable sanctions for breaking the rules. Due to the minor overspend breach, the Grove-based squad has agreed with the CCA that the outcome will be a financial penalty and a 1.5 per cent reduction in wind tunnel and CFD testing over the next 12 months.

The James Vowles-led team unintentionally exceeded the cap by £627,000 – 0.48 per cent — last year.

Neither Williams nor Alpine have disclosed the amount of the fines imposed by the FIA for their respective indiscretions.

The other nine Formula 1 teams, including fledgling outfit Cadillac, and the five power unit manufacturers were all found in compliance with the regulations for the 2025 reporting period.

[Article continues below]

What is the FIA cost cap for F1?

F1 has been governed by an FIA-mandated cost cap since 2021, introduced to curb out-of-control spending and level the playing field.

Teams report their annual spending to the FIA against a base limit that started at $145 million and stands at $215 million for 2026, when the rules were widened to cover more costs.

Driver salaries and marketing costs sit outside the cap, as do the salaries of each team's three highest-paid employees other than its drivers.

Red Bull exceeded the 2021 cap by £1.86 million and received a $7 million fine and a 10 per cent cut in their aerodynamic testing allowance for a year.

Aston Martin and Williams stayed within the cap but committed procedural breaches in 2021, and Aston Martin recorded a further procedural breach in 2024.

Despite the intentions behind the cost cap, it has drawbacks that have been a hot topic in F1 of late; Williams team principal Vowles has argued that the cap can entrench the leading teams' advantage because rivals with outdated factories must divert money from car development to pay for improvements.

title: Lewis Hamilton refutes old F1 rival's Ferrari claims: 'I don't see that'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has rejected claims made about Ferrari by Sebastian Vettel in his new documentary.

Vettel raced for Ferrari between 2015 and 2020, coming close to winning the 2017 and 2018 titles for the Scuderia in fights against Hamilton, then at Mercedes, but ultimately fell short.

Vettel's time at Ferrari was dominated by internal politics, with Luca di Montezemolo, who had signed him, leaving before he joined in 2015, whilst Sergio Marchionne and Maurizio Arrivabene treated him as merely an "employee" rather than in the mould of Michael Schumacher.

In his new documentary, which Hamilton took part in, Vettel claimed that during his time, the mechanics were not allowed to have fun owing to the pressures of needing to succeed, and that team leadership did not want them to listen to music.

These claims were put to Hamilton, now in his second season with the Scuderia.

"I don't see that," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"I see two other teams that I've been in; the energy, I think, has been similar in the sense of: they're just focused; they really, really want to win. I think the focus and the passion is as high as it can be.

"We don't have a speaker in our garage playing crazy music like the garage next door [Red Bull], but no, I think there's a good vibe, there's a good energy.

"I think we're enjoying, of course, much more this year; last year was not so much fun for any of us, but we've come a long way."

Both Hamilton and Leclerc have endured periods of tension this year, including during last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

While the harmony inside the team appears to be rocked, Hamilton insisted the team has come a long way when it comes to on-track improvements.

"We're fighting for second in the constructors' championship," he said.

"We've come a really, really long way, and this is just the beginning. There's more to come."

title: 2026 F1 Qatar Grand Prix weather forecast
excerpt:
F1 heads into round 22 of the season with no weather uncertainty hanging over the Qatar Grand Prix.

Forecasts for Lusail International Circuit point to entirely dry conditions across all three days, meaning any strategic variation this weekend will come from tyre management rather than changeable skies.

Friday's track action is expected to open with air temperatures around 27°C for free practice 1, dropping to roughly 24°C once free practice 2 gets underway under the floodlights.

Humidity is forecast to sit near 63 per cent, with wind gusts of 10 to 20 km/h the only disruptive factor drivers may need to account for. Precipitation risk has been put at effectively zero for both sessions.

Saturday brings a continuation of the settled pattern, with daytime highs again reaching around 29°C and overnight temperatures falling to 19°C.

Free practice 3 is expected to run in ambient conditions close to 25°C, before qualifying cools further to approximately 22°C as the sun disappears.

Humidity is projected to ease slightly to 56 per cent, with winds calming to around 5 km/h by the time the lights come on for the top-10 shootout.

Race day is forecast to sit between 22°C and 24°C, with clear skies and relatively calm winds. Humidity, however, is expected to climb sharply to as much as 80 per cent, a shift that typically accompanies the steep drop in track temperature after sunset at Lusail.

That cooling has technical consequences, airelli has nominated its hardest compound range for the weekend, the C1, C2 and C3, and reintroduced a 27-lap maximum stint length per set.

Over a 57-lap race distance, that limit rules out any one-stop strategy outright, leaving every driver committed to at least two pit stops regardless of how conservatively they manage their tyres through Lusail's sustained high-speed corners.

title: Fernando Alonso delivers damning verdict after Las Vegas misery
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has stated the Las Vegas Grand Prix was the "worst race of the year" for Aston Martin's straight-line speed performance.

As the F1 campaign winds down, Aston Martin arrived at Las Vegas knowing it was a venue at which it was likely to struggle.

The performance from its Honda power unit has been lacking all year, leaving the team vulnerable down long straights.

With Aston Martin on full throttle at over 70 per cent of the lap at the Las Vegas Strip Circuit, it made for a very painful race.

Alonso was running in 18th place when he retired his car, one corner from the finish line.

"Yeah, the engine was down from the beginning of the race," Alonso told media including RacingNews365.

"We saw yesterday already in qualifying that the engine was down, and in the whole race it was down.

"I was losing a lot of time on the straights, not only to the rest of the field, but also to Lance.

"In the last two laps, the engine completely gave up."

It left Alonso to conclude that it was his worst race of the year, as he claimed to be losing several seconds down the straights.

"I was not fighting," he said. "I was losing two seconds or three seconds on the straights. I was gaining two seconds in the corners.

"I was just trying to follow the train of cars. The car was very good in the corners, much better than the fights that we had around us.

"But on the straights, this was probably the worst race of the year."

title: F1 broadcasters split over Middle Eastern grand prix coverage
excerpt:
Despite the ongoing unrest in the Middle East, Formula 1 is set to arrive as usual in Lusail this weekend for the Qatar Grand Prix. However, a number of TV networks will not be present.

Formula 1 arrives at the Lusail International Circuit this weekend for the Qatar Grand Prix, but not every usual broadcaster is sending staff to the F1 paddock.

Due to the continued unrest in the Middle East, some key players in the F1 media landscape have chosen to skip the weekend, instead opting to provide coverage of the round remotely.

The geopolitical situation between the United States, Israel and Iran has heavily affected the original F1 schedule, with a revised calendar required due to the war between the three nations, and the subsequent instability in the Middle East region at large.

The Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Grands Prix were both postponed earlier in the year. The former was delayed and relocated to Malaysia, and the latter was cancelled altogether.

The final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi have been monitored closely ever since.

It was eventually decided that both grands prix will go ahead as planned, after F1 explored and readied Imola as a contingency option. Teams and drivers have therefore arrived in Lusail and are making their final preparations for the weekend.

It is worth highlighting that with both the drivers' and constructors' championships already settled, there is, naturally, less to play for in the final two rounds of the campaign. As such, numerous written media outlets will not have journalists in the paddock as usual.

But while the teams have made the trip as scheduled, some of the championship's biggest broadcasters have chosen not to attend.

A handful of rights holders, including Viaplay, Sky Sports and Canal+, usually send a full crew of reporters to every round, with several European broadcast teams typically present trackside.

[Article continues below]

Grand Prix

Qatar GP

Split among the major broadcasters

That number will be noticeably smaller in Qatar, with some outlets deciding against sending staff to Lusail.

Dutch broadcaster Viaplay will cover the weekend as normal, meaning viewers in the Netherlands are unlikely to notice any difference.

Elsewhere, the picture looks very different. RacingNews365 understands that Sky Sports Germany will not be broadcasting from Lusail at all, instead covering the race remotely from Munich.

French broadcaster Canal+ will follow the same approach, running its coverage out of Paris rather than attending the circuit.

Sky Sports F1, the English-language arm of Sky's broader Formula 1 coverage, will be on the ground in Qatar as usual, and RacingNews365 understands that Sky Sports Italia is also covering the race on site.

Smaller outlets have made similar calls to the two bigger absentees. Austria's ServusTV will not be present in the paddock, and reports indicate that Spain's DAZN will also not be in the paddock.

Of the major broadcasters, then, the split is clear: Sky Sports F1 and Sky Sports Italia are making the trip, while Sky Sports Germany and Canal+ are not.

What happens for the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix remains unclear for some outlets, though Sky Sports Germany is expected to return to the paddock for that race.

title: Ferrari warned over bigger 'worry' if bust-ups continue into 2027
excerpt:
Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc have had several on-track incidents during the 2026 F1 season.

Former F1 driver Jolyon Palmer has stated Ferrari would be in "armageddon" if its drivers were contending for the title this year.

Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc have endured a number of on-track incidents this year, with the most prominent clash coming last Saturday night in Las Vegas.

Hamilton was spun around while battling Leclerc for sixth place, and the latter was deemed at fault by the stewards, who handed the Monegasque driver a 10-second time penalty.

Ferrari has endured a challenging campaign as the reset of the regulations did not see it leap into championship contention, while the tension between its drivers has added a further headache.

Palmer has warned that if the team is in a position to win the championship next year, it could suffer through its drivers fighting tooth and nail.

"It seems that there is no easy fix here to move one out of the team, and the worry is that these clashes have flared up over a podium in Monza, a win in Mexico and a measly sixth place in Vegas,” he wrote in his column for F1.

"If these two were fighting for the title it would surely be armageddon in the team by now.

"This year the Ferrari car hasn't been competitive enough for either driver to make that challenge, but it's easily conceivable that they can find the power they are missing for next year, which could propel the team to a genuine title challenge.

"They won't win anything with the drivers taking chunks out of each other like this though.

"Ironically the superstar lineup looks like it's becoming Ferrari's biggest Achilles' heel and I don't envy Fred Vasseur trying to sort it out before it really matters in 2027."

Ferrari benching a driver an 'unprecedented' move

Palmer has already suggested that Ferrari could look into benching one of its drivers, while former Haas team boss Guenther Steiner declared the team should look to implement a shock punishment to get its drivers in line.

However, Palmer has acknowledged that such a move for Ferrari would be "unprecedented", given how high of a status both of its drivers have.

"They need absolutely clear rules of engagement, but then is it a case of heavy fines if the drivers cross that line, or is it even the threat of a benching for a race?

"If these drivers were midfielders without huge brand value and individual clout it would be a much simpler decision.

"But it would be totally unprecedented for that level of internal sanction to be handed out to one of the greatest there has ever been, or to his incredibly gifted teammate who has been adored by the team for a long time.

"To me this partnership has now proven itself to be untenable, but Charles Leclerc has recently signed a new long-term deal and Lewis Hamilton is a seven-time champion who has just got back towards his best form."

title: Max Verstappen's punchy George Russell verdict backed by F1 fans as key advice issued
excerpt:
A significant majority of F1 fans believe Max Verstappen's comment about George Russell being "so far below my level" is correct.

The duo reignited their rivalry last weekend at the Las Vegas Grand Prix after they clashed during the final practice session, resulting in a war of words throughout the weekend.

Russell stated that "someone had to stand up" to Verstappen and that the Dutchman shouldn't be allowed to "walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else."

After his victory on Sunday, Verstappen launched his own response in a scathing criticism of his rival, taking a jab at Russell's poor season and stating his driving was not comparable to the four-time champion.

RacingNews365 asked you, the fans, if Verstappen's remark about Russell being "so far below" Verstappen's level was the right assessment.

Just over 85 per cent of those who responded to the poll felt that Verstappen's point of view was correct.

Some pundits suggested that Russell should focus more on improving his on-track results rather than get into a new feud with Verstappen.

That prospect was also put to fans, and on that occasion, 83.5 per cent of those who responded to the suggestion answered that Russell should back off from aggravating Verstappen, with only 16.5 per cent thinking he is right to stand up to the Red Bull driver.

title: Major Mercedes concern raised after seismic Red Bull F1 improvement
excerpt:
1997 F1 champion Jacques Villeneuve has warned Mercedes about its position in the 2027 pecking order after Red Bull's late-season improvement.

At the start of the current campaign under fresh technical regulations, Mercedes was cruising out front and won eight out of the opening 10 grands prix.

While rival teams eventually caught up, the Brackley-based squad eased to double championship success, wrapping up both titles with several rounds remaining on the calendar.

However, it has won just once in the last six races, with Red Bull winning four times in that period with Max Verstappen.

The four-time champion has enjoyed a much stronger second half of the campaign and is currently on a nine-race streak of consecutive podium finishes.

Villeneuve stated the strong form is setting him up for a title challenge next year.

“The second half has been preparation for next year,” Villeneuve told Sky F1.

“The first half was figuring out the new rules. They've made a step forward. He [Verstappen] has understood those rules really well.

“Mercedes has made a big step back, and it's tough to imagine where they'll be at next year.

“They didn't get used to racing this year because they were just running at the front. That'll be a bit different.

“But he [Verstappen] stands out. He's really above the rest right now.”

Verstappen verbal attack done to 'hurt' Russell

One of the biggest talking points from last weekend's event in Las Vegas was Verstappen's war of words with George Russell, as he declared after the grand prix that the Mercedes driver was “so far below my level” after the two took home very different results.

Addressing the fighting words from Verstappen, Villeneuve said: “The comments are there to hurt, to put George in place.

“From the outside, you just have to laugh and find the fun in the words that are being used.

“There was no bad word at all, no insulting word.”

title: McLaren boss delivers 'grim place' verdict after significant overhaul
excerpt:
McLaren has undergone some significant changes since the arrival of Zak Brown 10 years ago.

McLaren CEO Zak Brown has admitted the McLaren team was a "grim place" when he took over 10 years ago.

The Woking-based squad was struggling for form in the early years of the turbo-hybrid era with Honda, with more painful years following soon after Brown's arrival.

However, it began to turn around its performance in 2019 and broke a five-year podium drought towards the end of the campaign.

It continued to grow and enjoyed back-to-back constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025, while also winning the drivers' championship with Lando Norris last year.

Brown gave credit to those in leadership positions at McLaren for turning the team's form around.

"It's ultimately been turned around by all the people at McLaren," Brown told media including RacingNews365.

"They've done an outstanding job. It was a pretty grim place when I joined at the end of 2016.

"It's been remarkable, the turnaround. A few championships since then, we've won 24-plus races, having a lot of fun, which I think is very important.

"The culture, the energy of the racing team has been outstanding."

[Article continues below]

McLaren wary of challenge ahead

Having enjoyed a highly successful period across 2024 and 2025, the start of the new regulation cycle has proven challenging for McLaren.

It has endured fluctuations in form this year but has still managed to get on the top step of the podium with Norris.

However, Brown insisted McLaren has its work cut out to remain a permanent presence at the front of the grid.

"Great to be back at the front on a regular basis, and now we've found it's just as hard to stay at the front. But it's been a great quest, as we call it.

"A journey is kind of how you get to work every day. A quest is flying to the moon, and I think being successful in Formula 1 is much more a quest than a journey. A great quest."

title: Toto Wolff explains why Mercedes never got to use secret F1 'weapon'
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has explained how Mercedes was unable to use a "weapon" to steal victory away from Max Verstappen in the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

With the slipstream and tow extremely powerful in Sin City, race leader Verstappen quickly cottoned onto the fact that the grand prix would ultimately be decided in the final few hundred metres, through the kink on the run from the final chicane.

As such, it was required for a driver to be in second place exiting the Turn 14/15/16 chicane, with Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli running in second at the end of Lap 48 of 50, and primed to be in position to attack Verstappen.

However, at the end of Lap 49 and start of the final tour, Antonelli suddenly de-rated and slowed, allowing Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri of McLaren through to complete the podium, with the pressure alleviated on Verstappen, who took the flag 0.6s ahead of Norris.

Reflecting, Wolff revealed how a "weapon" was primed to be used by Mercedes in the final 400m of the race - one it never got the chance to use.

"At the end we were running the same deployment as the Alpines and McLarens," Wolff began to tell media, including RacingNews365.

"It is available for everyone, and I don't think it was exactly the same on the same laps, but everybody had the opportunity and was using it at certain stages.

"We had a weapon up our sleeve for the final 400 metres through the left kink, and I think [Antonelli] would have just saved it over the line to win the race.

"But obviously we lost that opportunity."

Wolff then went onto explain the events which stunted Antonelli's challenge.

"I think everything was set for an epic last lap in terms of energy deployment," Wolff began.

"And then unfortunately on the back straight, rather than passing Max, he lifted and that caused the battery to reapply and be totally depleted.

"He had no energy left."

[Article continues below]

Indy 500 x NASCAR x F1

With a record 352 overtakes and 35 for the lead, Wolff declared it was "great entertainment" and an unusual hybrid.

"These overtakes are great entertainment, and I think we saw a mega race, particularly for the Americans," he said.

"I guess it was the Indy 500, NASCAR, and Formula 1 mixed.

"I enjoyed it, but obviously within a [fraction] of a second, it can be gone if you do the wrong thing. [Antonelli] lifted, re-applied [the throttle], and the battery was empty."
